\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:results}

Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} fixed what was run: three models, four
scenarios, three frameworks, one sample per cell. This chapter asks what
it shows. Rather than walking through the 36 cells one at a time, it is
organised around six research questions that each aggregate across every
cell, model, and scenario collected, closing with a synthesis that draws
the six answers together and connects them back to the thesis's central
question (Section~\ref{sec:intro-missing}): \emph{can an LLM agent
iteratively optimise the deployment configuration of a backend application
on a Kubernetes cluster, guided by runtime performance feedback, to
maximise sustainable throughput under fixed infrastructure constraints?}

One methodological finding recurs across several of the research questions
below and is stated once, prominently, here rather than re-derived every
time it is relevant: \textbf{six of the 36 cells in this dataset were
touched by an LLM-provider billing or quota exhaustion event during
baseline code generation}, and every cell that never reached a working
baseline in this dataset was one of them. All six are attributable to a
single provider account: every one is \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s or, in
one case, \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s; none is \texttt{glm-5.2}'s. This is
narrower, and more asymmetric across models, than an earlier pass over
this same dataset found; Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} gives the full
accounting, and RQ1, RQ4, and RQ6 flag it locally wherever a number would
otherwise be misread as a capability or framework finding.


% ----- §5.1 Overview -----
\section{Overview of the Collected Data}
\label{sec:results-overview}

This chapter reports on \textbf{36 Kubernetes experiments} spanning three
models (\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, \texttt{gpt-5.5}, and \texttt{glm-5.2}),
fully crossed with the four scenarios and three frameworks of
Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} (12 cells per model), one sample per cell, run
under the \texttt{k8s-explore-refine} load profile with a ten-iteration
refinement budget ($N{=}10$).

All figures and summary statistics are produced by a single aggregation
script (\texttt{scripts/analysis/aggregate\_evaluation.py}), which walks
every experiment tree under \texttt{results/} and tabulates per-iteration
goodput, refinement lever, deployment-spec knobs, and recorded failure
records.
%
\textbf{Caveat on sample size.} Every cell in this chapter is a single
sample (one code-generation seed) run once (Section~\ref{sec:setup-procedure}).
The comparisons below are therefore \emph{descriptive}, not statistically
tested; medians and individual scenario-level points are shown side by
side throughout so the reader can judge dispersion directly rather than
trust a single summary statistic. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations}
returns to what this does and does not license us to claim, alongside the
billing-quota confound just introduced above.


% ----- §5.2 RQ1 -----
\section{RQ1: Does Iterative Refinement Improve Sustained Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq1}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{figures/eval/goodput_trajectories_grid.pdf}
  \caption{Sustained goodput per iteration, one panel per scenario$\times$framework
    cell, coloured by model. A missing line for a model means that model
    never produced a completed baseline bench for that cell; see
    Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} before reading a missing line as a
    capability gap.}
  \label{fig:results-trajectories-grid}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/baseline_vs_best_by_model.pdf}
  \caption{Median baseline (iteration \texttt{000}) vs.\ best-refined-iteration
    goodput, per model. Bars show the per-model median across cells; dots show
    every individual scenario$\times$framework cell.}
  \label{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} and Figures~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}--\ref{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
summarise all 36 cells at the model level.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Baseline vs.\ best-iteration goodput, by model (median over all
    cells; $n$ = number of scenario$\times$framework cells; ``healthy'' =
    baseline goodput $>0$). Two of the healthy-baseline cells behind the
    rightmost column (one \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} cell, one
    \texttt{gpt-5.5} cell) are still touched by the billing/quota
    confound of Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}; read that column together
    with the prose below, not in isolation.}
  \label{tab:results-rq1-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ cells & Median baseline & Median best & Baseline $>0$ & Median gain (healthy) \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 12 & 2{,}119.0 & 11{,}484.1 & 6 / 12 & $7.2\times$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 12 & 5{,}224.4 & 32{,}769.8 & 8 / 12 & $2.6\times$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 12 & 0.0       & 13{,}081.6 & 3 / 12 & $1.5\times$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Restricting to cells where the baseline already reached measurable
goodput, the ratio of best-iteration to baseline goodput is positive for
every model. \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s median healthy-baseline gain is $2.6\times$
(mean $15.6\times$, pulled up by a $75.4\times$ outlier on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}, where the baseline was
severely under-provisioned at 48 replicas and 1 full CPU each, against a
$1.2\times$ floor on \textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}, whose
baseline was already close to its achievable ceiling); \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
is $7.2\times$ over six healthy cells, ranging from $1.0\times$ to
$16.2\times$. The $1.0\times$ floor (\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask})
is a billing-confound artefact, though not quite in the way a coarser read
suggests: the baseline succeeded (1{,}868.1\,req/s) and the agent was given
two genuine code-refinement attempts, both of which regressed goodput to
exactly $0$; only then did every remaining attempt (iterations
\texttt{003}--\texttt{010}, eight consecutive tries) hit the same
provider-side quota error, so the trajectory was cut off during an actual
regression rather than never given a chance at all. Excluding this cell,
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s healthy-cell gain ranges $1.7$--$16.2\times$
with a median of $11.3\times$ ($n=5$).

\texttt{glm-5.2}'s median healthy-baseline gain is $1.5\times$ over three
cells (mean $6.0\times$), the lowest of the three models and a markedly
different figure from the $8.2\times$ an earlier pass over a smaller,
more billing-confounded slice of this same model's data reported: that
figure averaged exactly two cells, one of which (a $14.9\times$ gain on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}) is also present here. The
newly-available third healthy cell (\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask},
$1{,}837.5\to2{,}822.3$\,req/s, $1.5\times$) is a modest gain, and it is
this cell, not a change to the other two, that pulls the median down. This is
a reminder that with two-to-three healthy cells per model, small-sample
noise remains large even after a confound is resolved
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations}).

\paragraph{Refinement also rescues \emph{dead} baselines, almost
always.} In several cells the baseline never reaches a sustained plateau
at all: the adaptive load profile's warm-up step fails its health check
and the explore phase never starts (Section~\ref{sec:methods-load-profile}),
so sustained goodput is recorded as exactly $0$\,req/s even though some
requests were technically served during the failed warm-up window. Across
all three models, \textbf{15 of the 36 cells} start this way, and
\textbf{14 of those 15} recover to a benchmarkable, non-zero deployment
somewhere in their trajectory: all 4 of \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s dead baselines
recover (to $2{,}079.1$--$33{,}949.5$\,req/s), all 9 of \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
dead baselines recover (to $2{,}816.5$--$24{,}477.3$\,req/s), and 1 of
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s 2 dead baselines recovers
(\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}, $0\to4{,}053.0$\,req/s).
The sole cell that never recovers is \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}: no refinement iteration
across the full ten-iteration budget ever produced a passing bench. This
is a qualitatively different contribution than the tuning gains above: it
is the loop converting a \emph{non-functional} deployment into a
\emph{functional} one, not just a faster one, though, as the one
non-recovering case shows, not a guarantee. \texttt{glm-5.2}'s share of
dead baselines (9 of its 12 cells) is the largest of the three models;
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq4} returns to why once framework is brought
into the comparison.

\paragraph{Improvement is not perfectly monotonic.}
Individual iterations regularly regress goodput relative to the previous
successful iteration (visible as sawtooth segments in
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}). Because the framework only
advances the ``latest good'' lineage on \emph{successful} benches
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-outcome}), a regression is not silently
compounded: the next iteration's decision stage sees it in its feedback,
and in most cases observed here the trajectory recovers within one to two
iterations. Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} details one case where the
recovery takes longer and one where the final iteration of a cell's
ten-iteration budget is itself a regression to zero, i.e.\ recovery does
not always happen \emph{before} the budget runs out.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially every cell
that gets a genuine, uninterrupted opportunity to run: the exceptions
in this dataset trace to interrupted LLM access, not to the refinement
loop failing on its own terms. The size of the multiplicative gain is
dominated by how badly under-provisioned the baseline happened to be,
which is closer to a property of the baseline LLM call than of the
refinement loop itself, and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s comparatively modest
median gain looks more like a small-healthy-sample artefact (three cells,
one of them a modest $1.5\times$) than a capability difference, given
that its dead-baseline recovery rate is the strongest of the three models.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Yes, with two caveats.} Refinement improves goodput in every
model whenever it gets to run cleanly, and in a majority of cells it is
not a marginal improvement but the difference between a non-functional
and a functional deployment (14 of 15 dead baselines recover). The size of
the multiplicative gain is not a fixed ``refinement value-add'' comparable
across cells; and, separately, this dataset's completion figures remain
confounded by provider billing exhaustion for six cells
(Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}), so the ``Baseline $>0$'' column of
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} should not be read as a capability
ranking without that context.


% ----- §5.3 RQ2 -----
\section{RQ2: Which Refinement Lever Contributes More: Code or Deployment?}
\label{sec:results-rq2}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/code_vs_spec_delta.pdf}
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) relative to the previous
    \emph{successful} iteration, split by refinement lever. Steps whose
    predecessor had zero sustained goodput are excluded here (their delta
    is undefined as a percentage) and discussed under RQ1/RQ6.}
  \label{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Across all three models, 138 completed iterations chose \textbf{code}
refinement and 126 chose \textbf{deployment (spec)} refinement.
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq2-summary} and Figure~\ref{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
break the resulting per-step goodput change down by model and lever.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) by refinement lever and model
    (excludes steps whose predecessor had zero goodput).}
  \label{tab:results-rq2-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ & median & mean & $n$ & median & mean \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 23 & $+4.9\%$ & $+12.4\%$ & 24 & $+2.6\%$ & $-2.0\%$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 35 & $+6.7\%$ & $+36.2\%$ & 43 & $+1.2\%$ & $-1.2\%$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 29 & $-0.2\%$ & $+0.9\%$  & 39 & $+0.6\%$ & $-7.0\%$ \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 87 & $+3.0\%$ & $+18.2\%$ & 106 & $+0.9\%$ & $-3.5\%$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Code refinement has a heavier tail; spec refinement is a
smaller, noisier knob that occasionally backfires outright.} Pooled
across all models, median per-step change is modest for both levers
(code $+3.0\%$, spec $+0.9\%$), but the \emph{mean} diverges sharply
(code $+18.2\%$, spec $-3.5\%$). The gap is driven by a handful of large
code-side recoveries, single-step jumps of up to $+334.9\%$
(\texttt{gpt-5.5}), $+239.0\%$ (\texttt{glm-5.2}), and $+194.9\%$
(\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}), where a code change fixed a latent
correctness or connection-handling bug that no amount of replica or
resource tuning could have addressed. Deployment refinement, once the
application is already healthy, behaves like what it is designed to be: a
marginal capacity/placement adjustment that is negative on average
(pooled spec mean $-3.5\%$) and, in five recorded steps spread across five
different \texttt{glm-5.2} cells, negative in the most extreme way
possible: a working deployment driven all the way back to zero sustained
goodput by a single spec change (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} details
one such case). \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s mean code effect ($+12.4\%$) is
noticeably lower than \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s ($+36.2\%$) despite a comparable
median; part of this gap is the billing-affected cells, whose few
surviving iterations are noisier than a clean trajectory's would be
(Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}), so this specific comparison should be
treated as provisional.

\texttt{glm-5.2}'s pooled numbers looked, in a smaller and more
billing-confounded sample, like a simply flatter version of the other two
models' profile. With \texttt{glm-5.2}'s sample roughly doubled (29 code
and 39 spec steps, up from 14 and 17) now that six more of its cells run
cleanly, that reading does not survive: \texttt{glm-5.2} does have a
heavy code-refinement tail (up to $+239.0\%$, the same connection-pooling
fix discussed in Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}), and its spec-refinement
mean ($-7.0\%$) is the most negative of the three models, not the least,
pulled down by the five zero-goodput regressions just mentioned. What
does hold up is that \texttt{glm-5.2}'s \emph{typical} (median) step, on
either lever, is smaller than the other two models' (code median
$-0.2\%$ vs.\ \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s $+4.9\%$ and \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s
$+6.7\%$), so ``smaller, more conservative typical edits, occasionally
punctuated by a large correctness fix or a complete regression'' is a more
accurate description of \texttt{glm-5.2}'s profile than ``a flatter
version of the same lever asymmetry.''

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
This supports the framework's decision to keep code and deployment
refinement mutually exclusive per iteration
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}): the two levers act on genuinely
different failure classes across all three models. Code refinement does
more of the heavy lifting for correctness-adjacent bottlenecks (the
same class of bug BaxBench's original single-container evaluation cannot
even observe, since it never applies load; Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}),
while deployment refinement does comparatively fine-grained capacity
tuning once the application is already sound, at the cost of an
occasional complete backfire that a code change essentially never
produces in this dataset (code refinement's minimum observed step is also
$-100\%$, but it is a rare tail event rather than five-out-of-39 steps for
any model).

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains and
carries most of the ``fix a broken deployment'' work; deployment
refinement is a smaller, more consistent-on-median but higher-tail-risk
capacity knob, occasionally regressing a healthy deployment to zero.}
This division of labour now holds, with a larger and cleaner sample, for
all three models, including \texttt{glm-5.2}, whose flatter \emph{median}
profile on both levers is real but no longer supports the earlier
reading that the code/spec asymmetry itself was absent for this model.


% ----- §5.4 RQ3 -----
\section{RQ3: How Do the Models Compare?}
\label{sec:results-rq3}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/completion_funnel.pdf}
  \caption{Run completion status per model, counted over scenario$\times$framework
    cells. ``Aborted at baseline'' = baseline code or spec generation never
    produced a completed bench. \textbf{Every instance of this category in
    this dataset is a billing/quota artefact confined to
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}}, not a model failure; see text.
    ``Completed full trajectory'' = reached iteration 010.}
  \label{fig:results-completion-funnel}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence: the raw completion numbers.}
\texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2} both reach a completed baseline
bench in \textbf{12/12} cells and complete the full ten-iteration
trajectory in \textbf{12/12}. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} reaches a completed
baseline in \textbf{8/12} cells, completing the full trajectory in all 8
that reach one.

\paragraph{Evidence: what actually explains the gap.}
Reading those numbers as a capability ranking would still be a mistake,
though the mistake is now confined to one model rather than two. All 4 of
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s non-baseline cells are its
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells (\textsc{BranchWeave}, \textsc{ClickCount},
\textsc{Petstore}, and \textsc{Recipes}), and all 4 show an identical
failure signature: ten consecutive \texttt{llm\_call}-kind attempts at
baseline code generation, every one carrying Anthropic's verbatim
``credit balance is too low to access the Anthropic API'' error, and zero
functional-test or other correctness signal. None of the four ever
produced a billed LLM call (no \texttt{llm\_cost\_ledger.json} exists for
any of them): the provider rejected every attempt before it could
generate billable output, so these cells cost \$0.00 and were never, in
any meaningful sense, attempted. A fifth \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} cell
(\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}) reached baseline and
completed two code-refinement iterations before hitting the same error on
every one of the remaining eight (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}). A sixth
cell, this time \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s \textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix},
hit the same class of error repeatedly from iteration \texttt{003}
onward and completed only 3 of a possible 11 iterations before the budget
ran out. \texttt{glm-5.2} shows \textbf{zero} \texttt{llm\_call} failures
anywhere in its 12 cells: the six cells that previously failed to reach
baseline for this model are fully resolved in this snapshot.

\paragraph{Cost.} Measured LLM spend (Table~\ref{tab:setup-model-cost})
still shows \texttt{glm-5.2} roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per
\emph{attempted} cell than \texttt{gpt-5.5} or \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}.
Reporting \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s spend as a simple total-over-12-cells
average would still conflate ``efficient'' with ``never got to spend'',
as an earlier pass over this chapter flagged: four of its twelve cells
accrued exactly \$0 (rejected calls are not billed), so its per-cell
figure is now reported over the eight cells that were actually billed
anything (\$47.11 / 8 $=$ \$5.89/cell), not over all twelve
(\$47.11 / 12 $=$ \$3.93/cell, the figure an unqualified average would
give). \texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2} needed no such adjustment:
every one of their cells accrued a non-zero, billed cost.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
With the confound now resolved for \texttt{glm-5.2} and unchanged for
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, this dataset supports a narrower but more useful
statement than either ``these three models differ in completion
reliability'' or ``we cannot compare them at all'': \texttt{gpt-5.5} and
\texttt{glm-5.2} both reach a working baseline on 12/12 attempted cells,
and \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} reaches one on 8/8 cells where the provider
account did not reject every attempt. The remaining open question is
specifically about \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s four
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells, not about the three-model comparison in
general.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{This dataset still does not support a completion-rate ranking
that includes \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells},
because the observed gap there traces entirely to a provider account
running low on funds during data collection, not to generation quality.
What it does now support, that an earlier pass over a more confounded
slice of this data could not: \texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2} are
directly comparable on completion rate (12/12 each) and on cost-per-cell,
and both reach a working baseline and go on to refine it substantially on
every cell attempted (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}). Closing the
remaining gap requires re-running \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s four
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells (and, ideally, its one truncated
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell) with a funded account;
this remains the single most important item in
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion-future-work}.


% ----- §5.5 RQ4 -----
\section{RQ4: Does Framework/Language Choice Affect Achievable Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq4}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/framework_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{Best goodput reached per framework (symlog $y$-axis), split by
    model. Each dot is one scenario cell; the horizontal bar is the
    per-model median for that framework. The empty
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} bar on \textsc{Rust-Actix} is the billing/quota
    confound of Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}, not a framework-difficulty
    finding; \texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells, previously also
    empty for the same reason, are now fully populated.}
  \label{fig:results-framework-comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
\textsc{Go-net-http} reaches the highest goodput for all three models
(medians $56{,}048$\,req/s for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, $36{,}844$\,req/s for
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, $17{,}845$\,req/s for \texttt{glm-5.2}),
consistent with a compiled, natively-concurrent runtime under CPU-bound
load. \textsc{Python-Flask} trails on all three models (medians
$20{,}260$, $2{,}961$, and $8{,}745$\,req/s respectively; the
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} figure is pulled down by its
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} dead cell,
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}), in line with the expected throughput
ceiling of a single-process WSGI stack under \texttt{gunicorn}, even
after the agent tunes replica count and worker/pool sizing.

\textsc{Rust-Actix} can now be compared for two of the three models:
\texttt{gpt-5.5} reaches a median of $33{,}147$\,req/s and
\texttt{glm-5.2} reaches $13{,}623$\,req/s, a real, if second-hand, gap
that this section returns to below. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} still cannot
be compared on this framework at all: it shows zero benchmarkable
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells out of four, and every one of those four cells'
recorded failures is the billing/quota confound of
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}, not a \texttt{functional\_test} failure:
the model was never given a completed LLM call to generate
\textsc{Rust-Actix} code from. \texttt{gpt-5.5} is otherwise comparable
across all three frameworks, and even one of its four
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells (\textsc{Recipes}) hit the same billing error
repeatedly before recovering (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}).

\paragraph{A genuine, previously-invisible \textsc{Rust-Actix} finding for
\texttt{glm-5.2}.} Now that \texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells
run past baseline, they show real, non-billing difficulty getting there:
7 of the dataset's 9 recorded \texttt{docker\_build} failures (Rust code
that fails to compile) are \texttt{glm-5.2} attempts at
\textsc{Rust-Actix} code, spread across three of its four cells in that
framework: five consecutive failed compiles on
\textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} before iteration
\texttt{006} first produces working code, two on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}, and one on
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}. A representative error
(\textsc{BranchWeave}, iteration \texttt{001}): \texttt{struct
`ManagerConfig' has no field named `statement\_cache\_capacity'}, a
connection-pool configuration field that does not exist in the crate
version the generated code targets. The one remaining
\texttt{docker\_build} failure belongs to \texttt{gpt-5.5}
(\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}, iteration \texttt{006}).
This is a genuine code-correctness signal specific to
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Rust-Actix} generation that a more
billing-confounded snapshot of this dataset could not show, because those
cells never previously got far enough to attempt a build at all; it is a
plausible, though not the only possible, contributor to
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s lower \textsc{Rust-Actix} median relative to
\texttt{gpt-5.5}'s.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
The \textsc{Go-net-http} $>$ \textsc{Python-Flask} ceiling ordering is
genuine and consistent across all three models, and is readable as a
runtime-throughput effect independent of refinement. The
\textsc{Rust-Actix} comparison is now meaningful for two of three models:
\texttt{gpt-5.5} clearly outperforms \texttt{glm-5.2} on this framework,
and the failure record gives a concrete, non-speculative reason to expect
at least part of that gap (\texttt{glm-5.2}'s repeated compile failures)
rather than leaving it as an unexplained ceiling difference.
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} remains the one model this chapter cannot say
anything about on \textsc{Rust-Actix}, for the same reason as before.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Framework sets an achievable-goodput ceiling}
(\textsc{Go-net-http} $>$ \textsc{Python-Flask} in every model with usable
data) \textbf{that refinement operates within, not around}, and this now
extends to a genuine \textsc{Rust-Actix} ceiling difference between
\texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2}, partly attributable to
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s harder time producing compilable \textsc{Rust-Actix}
code in the first place. The three-way comparison this chapter originally
set out to make is still not fully answerable: it requires re-running
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s four billing-affected \textsc{Rust-Actix}
cells, not further analysis of the existing ones.


% ----- §5.6 RQ5 -----
\section{RQ5: What Deployment Parameters Does the Agent Converge To?}
\label{sec:results-rq5}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Spec prompts intentionally omit recommended numeric ranges
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}), so any sensible-looking convergence in
\texttt{backend.replicas}, per-pod resource requests, or database
topology is evidence the agent is reading load-test and utilisation
feedback rather than falling back on defaults. The clearest example is
\texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} (the
$75\times$ case from RQ1):

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Spec-knob trajectory for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, \textsc{ClickCount},
    \textsc{Go-net-http} (selected iterations).}
  \label{tab:results-rq5-clickcount}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Iter.\ & Lever & Goodput (req/s) & Replicas & CPU req.\ & DB repl.\ & DB max\_conn \\
    \midrule
    000 & baseline & 1{,}285.1  & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    006 & code     & 23{,}670.6 & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    007 & spec     & 23{,}640.9 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    008 & code     & 90{,}653.8 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    009 & spec     & 91{,}392.6 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    010 & code     & 96{,}924.9 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Between iterations 006 and 010, the agent roughly \emph{sextuples}
replica count (48 $\to$ 320) while \emph{quartering} per-pod CPU request
(1000m $\to$ 250m), trading a few large pods for many small ones, and
drops database replicas from 3 to 1. For a scenario whose endpoints are a
near-stateless counter increment (Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios}),
this is the correct qualitative direction: per-request CPU cost is
negligible, so raw horizontal fan-out beats per-pod headroom, and the
extra Postgres read replicas the baseline provisioned were never
load-bearing. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} shows qualitatively similar
single-step spec jumps (up to $+167.5\%$; Table~\ref{tab:results-rq2-summary})
on its own cells, though a full knob-by-knob trajectory is not reproduced
here. \textbf{TODO: instrument \texttt{kubectl top} utilisation alongside
this table (available in \texttt{05-bench/diagnostics/}) to show the
CPU-utilisation signal that presumably drove this, rather than just
asserting it post hoc.}

Not every spec-refinement decision pays off, however:
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} gives a case where the stated rationale is
reasonable but the resulting deployment regresses to zero goodput, and
RQ2 above shows this is not a one-off: five separate spec-refinement
steps in this dataset (all on \texttt{glm-5.2} cells) collapse a healthy
deployment to zero.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Where the agent has enough successful iterations to work with, its
\texttt{spec.yaml} trajectory tracks the workload's actual scaling
characteristics rather than converging on generic defaults, which is the
behaviour the constrained-schema design of Section~\ref{sec:methods-design}
was intended to elicit.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The agent converges on workload-appropriate deployment parameters
when given the room to iterate}, but this chapter has one detailed
example, not a systematic audit; RQ6's counter-examples show this is a
tendency, not a guarantee, and RQ2's five zero-goodput spec regressions
show the failure mode is not rare.


% ----- §5.7 RQ6 -----
\section{RQ6: Failure Modes and Case Studies}
\label{sec:results-rq6}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/failure_taxonomy.pdf}
  \caption{Recorded \texttt{failure.json} occurrences by phase and kind,
    summed across all three models and all cells. \texttt{llm\_call}
    entries are dominated by the billing/quota confound of
    Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}; see text for the split.}
  \label{fig:results-failure-taxonomy}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Of \textbf{60} recorded failures, 24 are \texttt{02-code: functional\_test}
failures (baseline or refined code that fails \textsc{BaxBench}'s own
functional test suite before an image is ever built), split 2 / 12 / 10
across \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} / \texttt{gpt-5.5} / \texttt{glm-5.2}, and
these are the dataset's genuine code-correctness signal. A further
\textbf{21} are \texttt{llm\_call} failures (16 at the decision phase, 4
at the code phase, 1 at the spec phase). Tracing every one to its
underlying \texttt{llm\_error} text: 12 belong to
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} and are all the billing confound of
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} (the four permanently-stuck
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells plus eight failed retries on the
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell); 9 belong to
\texttt{gpt-5.5}, of which 8 are the same billing confound
(\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}) and the 9th is a different,
genuine stop condition: \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell hit its own configured
\texttt{--llm-max-cost} ceiling (\$20.22 spent against a \$20.00 cap) at
iteration 010's spec-refinement attempt: the framework's cost-tracking
safeguard (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}) doing exactly what it is
designed to do, not a reliability failure. \texttt{glm-5.2} records
\textbf{zero} \texttt{llm\_call} failures.

Two failure kinds that a more confound-dominated snapshot of this dataset
could not show are now visible in real numbers. \textbf{Nine
\texttt{docker\_build} failures} (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq4}) are
genuine compile-time code-correctness failures, concentrated on
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{Rust-Actix} generation (8 of 9; the remaining
one is \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s). \textbf{Two \texttt{04-deploy: unschedulable}}
failures, both on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell, both on consecutive
spec-refinement iterations (\texttt{005}, \texttt{006}): a proposed
spec's resource requests passed static validation
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}) but could not actually be scheduled onto
any node at apply time, pointing at a real gap between the static ``does
this fit on \emph{a} worker in isolation'' check and the cluster's actual
bin-packing state once other pods are already running on it. A related
but distinct pair, \textbf{two \texttt{04-deploy} failures recorded as
kind ``unknown''}, appear on \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} cell, also on consecutive
spec-refinement iterations (\texttt{005}, \texttt{006}); reading the
underlying diagnostic rather than trusting the coarse label shows a
different problem from the claude case above: \texttt{docker tag
failed: Error response from daemon: No such image}, i.e.\ the deploy
step tried to tag an image that the registry did not yet have, a
build/push propagation issue rather than a scheduling-capacity one. This
cell recovers by iteration \texttt{008}. Excluding all billing- and
cost-cap-related failures, the remaining signal is: 24
\texttt{functional\_test}, 9 \texttt{docker\_build}, 2
\texttt{unschedulable}, 2 deploy-phase image-tag failures, 1
decision-phase \texttt{llm\_parse}, and 1 \texttt{spec\_validation}:
40 of 60 recorded failures, up from roughly half in the more
billing-dominated earlier snapshot of this dataset, simply because fewer
cells are now being cut off before they can produce genuine signal.
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} contributes 16 of the 60 raw failures (12 of
them the billing artefact); \texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2}
contribute 22 each (9 of \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s are billing/cost-cap
artefacts; \emph{none} of \texttt{glm-5.2}'s are).

\paragraph{Case study: a connection-pooling bug invisible to
single-container evaluation.} \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} baseline reaches a completed
bench but records \textbf{0} sustained goodput: the adaptive profile's
warm-up step fails health checks and explore never starts. Postgres logs
from that run show the deployment producing roughly 937 errors during the
load window, dominated by two error classes:
\texttt{\small unnamed prepared statement does not exist} and
\texttt{\small bind message supplies N parameters, but prepared statement
requires M}. This is the classic symptom of a Go SQL driver using
server-side prepared statements against PgBouncer in \texttt{transaction}
pooling mode, where a prepared statement created on one physical
connection is invisible on the next pooled connection a later query lands
on. This bug is invisible to \textsc{BaxBench}'s original single-container
functional tests (which use a direct, unpooled connection) and only
manifests once the generated code is deployed behind the pooler this
framework introduces. Iteration~001 (code refinement) does not fix it
(goodput remains 0); iteration~002 (code refinement again, chosen freely
by the decision stage given the iteration~001 failure feedback) does,
jumping to $19{,}026.7$\,req/s. This is direct evidence that iterative
\emph{code} refinement, not deployment tuning, is the correct lever for
an infra-interaction bug the model could not have anticipated at
generation time, and that it can take more than one attempt. Unlike the
billing failures above, this one is a genuine, reproducible application
bug; it has nothing to do with LLM transport.

\paragraph{Case study: a plausible deployment decision that backfires.}
On the same cell, iteration~003's decision stage reasons as follows
(quoted verbatim from its \texttt{decision.json}):
\begin{quote}
\small
``The code is now well-optimized (0\% failures, 19K/s goodput) and the
bottleneck is purely infrastructure: Postgres hits 200/200 connections
with PgBouncer \texttt{cl\_waiting} reaching 311, and db-primary CPU
saturates at 16.7 cores. [...] We should add database replicas, enable a
read pooler, increase Postgres \texttt{max\_connections} and PgBouncer
\texttt{default\_pool\_size}, and potentially reduce over-provisioned
backend CPU to free cluster budget for more DB resources.''
\end{quote}
The reasoning is a coherent read of the previous iteration's diagnostics
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-bench}), and the resulting spec does exactly
what it describes: database replicas 1 $\to$ 3, \texttt{max\_connections}
200 $\to$ 300, backend CPU request 2000m $\to$ 500m. The resulting
deployment, however, regresses to \textbf{0} sustained goodput. The next
iteration (004, code) recovers to $20{,}494$\,req/s \emph{without}
reverting the topology change, so the regression is not explained by the
added replicas alone; most plausibly the simultaneous $4\times$ backend
CPU cut left the application under-provisioned for its own request
handling while the new DB topology was still stabilising. The cell goes
on to alternate lever choices through the rest of its budget, peaking at
$24{,}477.3$\,req/s at iteration~007 before settling at $21{,}722.2$\,req/s
by iteration~010, itself not a monotonic climb, with two further
consecutive code-refinement steps (iterations~008--009) that give back
part of the gain before the final spec step recovers it.
\textbf{Lesson for the framework, not just the model}: this iteration
changed four spec fields at once, which is consistent with the
single-lever-per-iteration design (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow})
but does not prevent \emph{multiple fields within one lever} from
changing simultaneously, which limits attribution within a spec-refinement
step the same way mixing code and spec changes would across steps. RQ2's
finding that five separate \texttt{glm-5.2} cells show this same
complete-collapse pattern on a spec step suggests this is not a one-off
either for this cell or this model.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
With the confound now resolved for all but one model, the remaining
evidence continues to support the reading that has held across both
versions of this chapter: essentially all \emph{genuine} attrition
happens at the code-correctness gate the agent is directly responsible
for (functional-test failures, and now also \texttt{docker\_build}
compile failures), and the cluster-execution path is close to, but not
quite, failure-free: the \texttt{unschedulable} and image-tag cases
are a real, if narrow, gap between static validation, build/registry
timing, and actual apply-time feasibility. The two case studies together
show the same lesson from opposite directions: code refinement can fix
bugs the model could not have anticipated (the pooling case), and a
single deployment decision can undo a healthy deployment even when its
diagnosis is correct, because the framework does not constrain how many
fields one spec-refinement step may touch (the backfire case), and
RQ2 shows this second failure mode recurring, not confined to one cell.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The dominant \emph{genuine} failure mode is upstream of
deployment}, in code correctness, now backed by a larger and more varied
genuine-failure sample (40 of 60 recorded failures, vs.\ roughly half in
the earlier, more confound-dominated snapshot) that additionally surfaces
a framework/language-specific correctness signal
(\texttt{glm-5.2}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} compile failures,
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq4}) the previous snapshot could not see at
all. With billing and cost-cap artefacts excluded, the cluster-execution
path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free: four deploy-phase failures
across two cells (two \texttt{unschedulable}, two image-tag) point at
real, fixable gaps in static spec validation and build/registry timing
respectively.


% ----- §5.8 Cross-Cutting Synthesis -----
\section{Cross-Cutting Synthesis}
\label{sec:results-synthesis}

Read together across all 36 cells, three models, and four scenarios,
four patterns recur consistently enough to generalise beyond any single
cell:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Correctness gates deployment, consistently.} Among
        genuine (non-billing) failures, the largest single source of
        attrition (RQ6) and the largest single-step goodput gains (RQ2)
        both trace back to code correctness, not deployment tuning. This
        holds across every model with usable data and is exactly the
        class of bug BaxBench's original single-container evaluation
        cannot observe (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}); it now also
        includes a framework-specific instance, \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
        repeated \textsc{Rust-Actix} compile failures (RQ4, RQ6).
  \item \textbf{Deployment refinement is real, bounded, and occasionally
        catastrophic.} Across every model, spec refinement's median
        per-step effect is small (RQ2: $+0.9\%$ pooled) and its mean is
        negative, never approaching code refinement's heavy positive
        tail; unlike code refinement, it also produces outright
        deployment-collapsing regressions with some regularity (five
        recorded zero-goodput spec steps, all \texttt{glm-5.2}).
        Deployment tuning is a genuine, but fundamentally
        marginal-capacity and higher-tail-risk, lever once an
        application is already correct, not a second path to the same
        order-of-magnitude gains code refinement can produce.
  \item \textbf{This dataset can now compare two of the three models'
        baseline-generation reliability directly, and the remaining gap
        is fully attributable and narrowly scoped.} \texttt{gpt-5.5} and
        \texttt{glm-5.2} are both 12/12 on completion and both refine
        substantially once alive (RQ1, RQ3); \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
        four missing cells and one truncated cell trace, cell for cell,
        to the same provider account running low on funds, not to
        generation quality, and are now the only unresolved piece of the
        model comparison (RQ3). \textsc{Go-net-http} $>$
        \textsc{Python-Flask} in achievable ceiling for every model, and
        \textsc{Rust-Actix} is now comparable for \texttt{gpt-5.5} vs.\
        \texttt{glm-5.2} specifically, with a real, partly-explained gap
        between them (RQ4).
  \item \textbf{The cluster-execution path is close to, but not quite,
        the one component that never appears as a bottleneck.} Four
        deploy-phase failures out of 60 recorded (and \emph{zero}
        bench-phase harness failures) is still strong evidence for the
        framework-owns-infrastructure design principle
        (Section~\ref{sec:methods-design}), with two concrete, narrow
        exceptions: static spec validation does not currently catch
        every case where a proposed deployment cannot actually be
        scheduled, and a build/registry propagation gap can leave a
        freshly-built image untaggable at deploy time.
\end{itemize}

The clearest lesson this pass adds to the previous one is again
methodological rather than purely empirical: re-running the aggregation
against a newer snapshot of the same dataset changed the completion
picture for one model entirely (\texttt{glm-5.2}, from 6/12 to 12/12) while
leaving another (\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}) and the third
(\texttt{gpt-5.5}) exactly as they were, which is only visible by
re-tracing every \texttt{llm\_error} string rather than trusting the
coarse \texttt{llm\_call} count. A coarse failure-kind label continues to
conflate genuine transport reliability, provider account state, and the
framework's own cost ceiling, and the three do not move together across
snapshots. Every model-comparison claim in this thesis that touches
completion rate has been re-checked against that distinction;
Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations} generalises the caution.


% ----- §5.9 Summary -----
\section{Summary}
\label{sec:results-summary}

Across all three models and all 36 scenario/framework cells collected:
%
\begin{itemize}
  \item iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially
        every cell that gets a genuine, uninterrupted attempt, and
        separately rescues 14 of the 15 \emph{dead} baselines observed
        into a working deployment (RQ1);
  \item code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains for
        all three models once a large enough sample is available,
        dominated by fixes to bugs that only manifest under load and
        cluster topology; deployment refinement is a smaller,
        lower-median but higher-tail-risk marginal capacity knob that
        occasionally collapses a healthy deployment outright (RQ2);
  \item \textbf{this dataset supports a direct completion-rate comparison
        between \texttt{gpt-5.5} and \texttt{glm-5.2} (12/12 each)}; the
        remaining gap involving \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} is fully
        explained by provider billing/quota exhaustion on four
        \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells and one truncated cell, not by
        generation quality (RQ3);
  \item \textsc{Go-net-http} sets the highest achievable-goodput ceiling
        among all three models; \textsc{Rust-Actix} is now comparable for
        \texttt{gpt-5.5} vs.\ \texttt{glm-5.2}, with a real gap partly
        explained by \texttt{glm-5.2}'s repeated \textsc{Rust-Actix}
        compile failures, while \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} remains
        incomparable on this framework due to the same billing confound
        (RQ4);
  \item where it converges, the agent's deployment-spec trajectory tracks
        workload characteristics sensibly (RQ5), though not every
        individual spec-refinement decision improves the outcome: five
        recorded steps collapse a healthy deployment to zero goodput
        outright, even when the stated rationale is sound (RQ6);
  \item nearly all \emph{genuine} attrition happens at the
        code-correctness gate the agent is responsible for, now
        including a framework-specific signal
        (\texttt{glm-5.2}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix} compile failures);
        the cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely,
        failure-free, with two narrow gaps (static-validation-vs-scheduling
        and build/registry propagation) accounting for
        four of 60 recorded failures (RQ6).
\end{itemize}

These findings are discussed further, including limitations and threats
to validity, in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}, and answered directly against
the thesis's research question in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
